title: Iraq masses troops on the Kuwaiti border and accuses it of stealing oil
what: Saddam Hussein has turned on his neighbour. Iraq accuses Kuwait of pumping far more oil than its OPEC quota allows, pushing prices down and costing Iraq billions it needs after eight years of war with Iran, and of drilling into the Rumaila field across the border. OPEC ministers met in late July and agreed to cut output; US crude rose from about 16.50 dollars early in the month to 20.57 at the end. Iraqi troops are reported to be gathering near the Kuwaiti frontier, which most observers read as pressure rather than a prelude to war. Oilfield shares such as Schlumberger rose 14%.
why: The prelude to the invasion of 2 August, restored after an accidental deletion on the review desk and strengthened at the curator's request: it should foreshadow next month without knowing it. The troop build-up and the Rumaila accusation are in the Gulf War article; the oil prices from EIA; the "pressure rather than war" reading was the common view at the time (sourced only as context in the Gulf War article).

title: Brent sinks toward $14
what: North Sea Brent fell to about $14 a barrel by the end of November and US crude to about $15, the lowest in five years, as OPEC members overproduce and demand is weak.
why: The quiet middle of the 1990s: cheap, plentiful oil and OPEC unable to enforce its quotas.

title: OPEC and its rivals cut together
what: On 23 March OPEC and non-OPEC producers including Mexico and Norway agreed to cut output by a combined 2.1 million barrels a day for one year. OPEC's revenues fell about 30% in 1998. US crude rose 23% in March to about $15.
why: The first effective joint cut with outsiders, the template for OPEC+ in 2016. It began the long climb.

title: Natural gas soars, California runs short of power
what: The US natural gas price at Henry Hub averaged $8.90 per million Btu in December, almost four times its level a year ago, while California's deregulated power market faces shortages and soaring prices. Crude meanwhile fell 20% in December to about $27 a barrel. Drillers and gas traders are the winners.
why: An energy spike in gas, not oil: it lifted gas-drilling services (Schlumberger +29%) and the energy trader Enron (+28%), whose role in the California crisis later became notorious.

title: Oil passes $55 on Chinese demand
what: US crude reached a record $56.37 a barrel on 26 October, up from about $33 in January. China's oil use is growing about 8% a year, OPEC has little spare capacity, and attacks on Iraqi pipelines continue. Earlier in the year, when oil reached $40, European finance ministers cut their growth forecasts.
why: The boom of the 2000s in full swing, driven by demand rather than a single supply shock.

title: Hurricane Katrina hits the Gulf oil coast
what: Hurricane Katrina struck the Gulf coast on 29 August. The region supplies about a tenth of US crude and refines almost half its gasoline; on 31 August eight Gulf refineries were still shut. US crude futures topped $70 a barrel, a record, and the government is releasing oil from the strategic reserve.
why: The hurricane showed how little slack was left in the system. US crude output fell by about a fifth from August to September.

title: Iran fears push oil toward $70
what: US crude rose 13% in January to $67.86 a barrel as the dispute over Iran's nuclear programme sharpened and attacks hit Nigeria's oil industry.
why: Geopolitical risk on top of tight supply. Oilfield services, the purest bet on high prices, had their best month: Schlumberger +31%.

title: Oil nears $100
what: US crude reached $99.16 a barrel on 20 November, up from about $50 in January. The dollar is weak, Chinese and Indian demand keeps growing, and money is pouring into commodities.
why: The run-up into the 2008 peak, while the US housing crisis was already under way.

title: The Gulf spill halts deep drilling
what: The Deepwater Horizon rig exploded on 20 April, killing 11 workers, and the well is still gushing tens of thousands of barrels a day into the Gulf of Mexico. The US government has imposed a six-month moratorium on deepwater drilling, stopping work on 33 rigs. US crude fell 14% in May to $74.
why: Drilling stopped in one of the world's main offshore areas, a direct hit for oilfield services: Schlumberger -21% in May.

title: Libya's war pushes Brent above $110
what: Revolt against Muammar Gaddafi has shut much of Libya's oil output, after uprisings in Tunisia and Egypt. Brent ended February at $112 a barrel. US crude, priced at Cushing, Oklahoma, is about $15 cheaper, an unusually wide gap.
why: Unrest in the Arab world helped keep Brent above $100 for most of the next three years. The Brent-WTI gap reflected growing inland US supply.

title: The shale boom
what: US crude output is near 8 million barrels a day, up from about 5.5 million in 2010, as horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing (fracking) open up shale formations. US oil imports are falling. Brent still costs about $110 a barrel.
why: The supply revolution that broke prices a year later and made the US the world's biggest producer.

title: OPEC refuses to cut
what: On 27 November in Vienna, Saudi oil minister Ali al-Naimi blocked calls from poorer OPEC members to cut output, saying the market should find its own level. US crude fell about 10% by 28 November to $65.94, down from $107 in June. US crude output is about 9.3 million barrels a day, up by two thirds in four years. ExxonMobil, which earned more than 32 billion dollars in 2013, fell 6%: every dollar off the oil price cuts its profit.
why: The decision that started the 2014-16 collapse: Saudi Arabia chose to squeeze high-cost shale. Schlumberger fell 13% in November.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OPEC (read 2026-10-03); https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=RWTC&f=D (read 2026-10-03); https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=MCRFPUS2&f=M (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010s_oil_glut (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 2 February 2015 (2013 and 2014 earnings), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408815000004/f8k4q991.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Paris climate deal, OPEC drops its ceiling
what: On 12 December nearly 200 countries adopted the Paris Agreement, pledging to hold global warming well below 2 degrees. Earlier in the month OPEC set aside its production ceiling altogether. US crude ended the year at $37.13 a barrel.
why: The energy transition becomes official policy, and OPEC admits it cannot defend the price. Two ideas, peak demand and a free-for-all in supply, frame the next decade.

title: Oil sinks to $26
what: US crude fell to $26.19 a barrel on 11 February, the lowest since 2003 and a quarter of its 2014 level. Sanctions on Iran were lifted in January. The OPEC basket price was $22.48 on 20 January. US output has started to fall.
why: The bottom of the shale bust; OPEC changed course within the year. Review 2026-10: 'bottoms' was hindsight.

title: OPEC and Russia agree to cut
what: At its 30 November conference OPEC agreed to cut about 1 million barrels a day for the first half of 2017, its first cut since 2008, with Russia and other non-members promising further reductions. Oil prices jumped and US crude ended the month near $49.
why: The birth of OPEC+, the Saudi-Russian alliance that has managed supply ever since.

title: Oil slumps 40% in three months
what: Brent fell from $86 in early October to about $50 at the end of December, and US crude to about $45, while US crude output reached new records near 12 million barrels a day.
why: Part of the December 2018 sell-off (market -9%); oilfield services lost a fifth, Schlumberger -20%.

title: Drones knock out half of Saudi output
what: Drone and missile attacks on 14 September hit Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq processing plant and the Khurais field, cutting 5.7 million barrels a day, about 5% of world supply. Brent futures jumped almost 20% on 16 September, the biggest jump since 1990, but Saudi Arabia moved quickly to restore output and prices gave back most of the gain.
why: The biggest supply outage in history at the time, and the market shrugged: with shale and spare capacity, supply shocks no longer lasted. Review 2026-10: 'restored within weeks' reached past the month.

title: Saudi-Russian price war as the world locks down
what: Russia rejected OPEC's call for deeper cuts on 6 March. Saudi Arabia answered by cutting its prices and announcing it would raise output from 9.7 to 12.3 million barrels a day. On 9 March oil fell about a quarter and stock markets crashed. As lockdowns spread, US crude fell to $20.48 on 18 March and ended the month down 54%. Schlumberger lost half its value in March and ExxonMobil 26 percent.
why: A supply war in the middle of the largest demand collapse ever. Part of the market's -13% month; oilfield services halved, Schlumberger -50%.

title: Oil goes negative
what: OPEC, Russia and others agreed on 9 to 12 April to cut output by 9.7 million barrels a day, about 10% of world supply. It was not enough: on 20 April the expiring May contract for US crude fell to minus $37 a barrel, as storage at Cushing, Oklahoma filled up and holders paid to get rid of oil. Brent fell to about $9 the next day. ExxonMobil had cut its 2020 capital spending by 30 percent, to about 23 billion dollars, on 7 April; its shares rose 22% as stocks rebounded.
why: The most extreme moment in oil-market history. Yet oil shares rebounded with the market (+13%) on the OPEC+ deal and hopes of reopening: Exxon +22%.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Russia%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_oil_price_war (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OPEC (read 2026-10-03); https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=RWTC&f=D (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 7 April 2020, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408820000028/f8k1q991.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Saudi cuts and a Texas freeze send oil past $60
what: US crude rose 18% in February to $61.55, the highest in more than a year, helped by a winter storm in Texas that froze wells and pipelines; gas at Henry Hub spiked to $23.86 on 17 February.
why: Oil recovered to pre-pandemic levels faster than expected; Exxon +21% and Schlumberger +26% in February.

title: The IEA says: no new oil fields
what: On 18 May the International Energy Agency published a roadmap to net-zero emissions by 2050. In its pathway no new oil and gas fields are approved beyond those already committed, and world oil demand falls to about 24 million barrels a day by 2050, from about 90 million in 2020.
why: The energy transition's sharpest statement from a mainstream body; it shaped investor and boardroom pressure on oil companies, and critics later blamed underinvestment for the 2022 squeeze.

title: Tight supply and Russian troops push oil toward $90
what: US crude rose 18% in January to $89.16 a barrel, the highest since 2014, as demand recovers while OPEC+ adds supply only gradually, and more than 100,000 Russian troops are massed around Ukraine. Europe has been in a gas crisis since the autumn.
why: Oil shares surged while tech fell (market -5%): Schlumberger +30%, Exxon +24%.

title: Russia invades Ukraine, oil tops $100
what: Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February. Brent passed $100 a barrel for the first time since 2014 and ended the month at $103. Europe, which depends on Russian gas, faces the larger energy problem.
why: The start of the 2022 energy shock that drove inflation to 40-year highs.

title: Brent hits $133, the US bans Russian oil
what: Brent reached $133 a barrel on 8 March, the day the US banned imports of Russian oil. On 31 March the US announced it would release 1 million barrels a day from its strategic reserve for 180 days, the largest release ever. US gasoline averaged $4.22 a gallon in March.
why: The peak of the war spike; the record reserve release and recession fears pulled prices back over the following months.

title: US gasoline at a record
what: US regular gasoline averaged $4.93 a gallon in June, a record, and Brent was near $129 on 8 June. The EU has agreed to ban seaborne imports of Russian crude by December.
why: Peak pain at the pump; prices fell from here as central banks raised rates hard.

title: OPEC+ cuts 2 million barrels a day
what: On 5 October OPEC+ agreed to cut its output target by 2 million barrels a day, its first cut since 2020; the decision revived calls in the US Congress for an anti-cartel law (NOPEC). US crude rose from $84 to $93 in the first week of October. Russia stopped gas deliveries through Nord Stream in September, and the pipelines were damaged by sabotage on 26 September.
why: OPEC+ showed it would defend $80-90. Energy shares had their best month of the cycle: Schlumberger +45%, Exxon +27%.

title: COP28 calls for moving away from fossil fuels
what: The UN climate conference in Dubai ended on 13 December with the first agreement that names all fossil fuels, calling for a move away from them in a just, orderly and equitable manner, and a tripling of renewable capacity by 2030. Brent is about $78 a barrel; OPEC+ members, Saudi Arabia above all, are holding back output to support the price.
why: A milestone in the transition, hosted by an oil producer. Demand kept growing all the same.

title: Maduro captured, Iran in turmoil
what: US forces captured Venezuela's president Nicolas Maduro on 3 January, after a US blockade of sanctioned Venezuelan tankers since December. In Iran, security forces violently suppressed mass protests, and the US is building up forces in the region. US crude rose 13% in January to $64.50, from about $56 early in the month.
why: The first signs of the 2026 shock; oil shares jumped (Schlumberger +26%, Exxon +18%). How much of that was Venezuela, Iran or other causes is not settled.

title: A US-Iran memorandum, oil back to $70
what: The US and Iranian presidents signed a memorandum on 17 June to end the war and the blockades. Brent fell from about $100 at the start of June to about $70 at the end, near its pre-war level, although Iran closed the strait again on 20 June citing Israeli violations.
why: The market bet that the crisis was over; it was premature.
